correlates.name: Hypertensive Emergency
correlates.pathophysiology: severe blood pressure elevation requiring controlled, titratable reduction; overshoot must be avoided because an abrupt fall provokes a sympathetic reflex.
correlates.treatment: nicardipine or clevidipine by slow I.V. infusion (Slide 19). A DHP CCB is combined with labetalol or esmolol to prevent reflex tachycardia.

correlates.name: Variant (Vasospastic / Prinzmetal) Angina
correlates.pathophysiology: coronary artery vasospasm rather than fixed obstruction.
correlates.treatment: CCBs are first-line and may be combined with nitroglycerin (Slide 20). CCBs induce coronary vasodilation.

correlates.name: Exertional (Stable) Angina
correlates.pathophysiology: fixed coronary obstruction; ischemia appears when demand rises.
correlates.treatment: beta blockers are first-line; a BB plus a DHP CCB is more effective than either agent alone (Slide 20). Non-DHP CCBs are used for patients who do not tolerate a beta blocker, because of their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects.

correlates.name: Unstable Angina / Acute Coronary Syndrome
correlates.treatment: a DHP CCB only when combined with a beta blocker. A non-DHP may be used only in patients who (1) do not tolerate a beta blocker, (2) do not have left ventricular dysfunction, and (3) show no signs of disturbed AV conduction (Slide 20).

correlates.name: Supraventricular Tachyarrhythmias
correlates.treatment: verapamil and diltiazem in hemodynamically stable patients, to slow automaticity and slow conduction through the AV node, which slows the ventricular response (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
correlates.treatment: nimodipine, which is lipophilic and produces cerebral artery vasodilation, to reduce the incidence and severity of ischemic deficits (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Raynaud Phenomenon
correlates.treatment: long-acting DHP CCBs. At least a moderate reduction in the intensity of attacks and prevention of tissue loss is achievable in most patients (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Preterm Labor (Tocolysis)
correlates.treatment: nifedipine, for 48 hours only, to suppress premature contractions in preterm labor at 24-34 weeks (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Dihydropyridine-Induced Peripheral Edema
correlates.presentation: pitting edema, worst in the lower extremities and feet because of gravity.
correlates.pathophysiology: vasodilation produces pre-capillary (arteriolar) dilation with post-capillary reflex constriction, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and permeability, so fluid redistributes into the interstitium (Slide 22).
correlates.treatment: dose reduction or a change of agent.

correlates.name: Digoxin Toxicity from a Verapamil Interaction
correlates.pathophysiology: P-glycoprotein normally pumps digoxin out of the systemic circulation into the gut and into the renal tubule. Verapamil blocks P-gp, so less digoxin is removed at both sites and plasma levels climb (Slide 25).
correlates.treatment: avoid the combination; if it is used, monitor digoxin levels closely.

correlates.name: Congestive Heart Failure
correlates.pathophysiology: sustained sympathetic activation is initially compensatory but ultimately worsens heart failure.
correlates.treatment: beta blockers, started at low dose in stable patients.

correlates.name: Hyperthyroidism and Thyroid Storm
correlates.presentation: palpitations, tachycardia, tremulousness, anxiety, heat intolerance. Thyroid storm can cause supraventricular tachycardia and sudden death.
correlates.pathophysiology: hyperthyroidism raises basal metabolic rate and enhances organ sensitivity to catecholamines, associated with an increased number of beta adrenergic receptors (Slide 49).
correlates.treatment: beta blockers ameliorate the symptoms and control pulse rate, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation.

correlates.name: Glaucoma (Topical Ophthalmic Beta Blockers)
correlates.pathophysiology: beta receptors of the eye are largely beta-2, located in the ciliary body epithelium and blood vessels (Slide 50).
correlates.treatment: topical beta blockers decrease intraocular pressure, presumably by decreasing production of aqueous humor and/or ocular blood flow, which decreases the ultrafiltration responsible for aqueous production.

correlates.name: Situational / Performance Anxiety ("Stage Fright")
correlates.presentation: extreme anxiety or panic in specific situations, with sympathetic manifestations - palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, muscular tension, trembling, flushing, sweating, dry mouth (Slide 51).
correlates.treatment: a low dose of propranolol taken about an hour before the performance reliably decreases the somatic manifestations, such as the pounding heart and trembling hands and voice.

correlates.name: Hypoglycemia Unawareness in an Insulin-Treated Patient
correlates.presentation: the patient does not recognize that he or she is dropping into hypoglycemia.
correlates.pathophysiology: two hits (Slide 52). Beta-2 blockade blocks the hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis that would raise blood sugar, and beta blockade blunts the adrenergic warning symptoms - tremor, tachycardia, nervousness.

correlates.name: Beta Blocker Withdrawal Syndrome
correlates.presentation: nervousness, tachycardia, increased blood pressure (potentially higher than before treatment ever started), increased intensity of angina, and increased risk of sudden death…
correlates.pathophysiology: chronic blockade causes upregulation or supersensitivity of beta adrenoceptors - more receptors expressed on the plasma membrane. Abrupt discontinuation exposes that enlarged pool to circulating norepinephrine and epinephrine (Slide 54).
correlates.treatment: never stop a beta blocker abruptly - taper gradually over a week or more, depending on how long the patient has been treated and the patient's age .

drugs.name: Verapamil
drugs.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blockade acting on vessels and heart alike, depressing sinus node automaticity and slowing AV conduction with the strongest frequency-dependent block of the class
drugs.indication: Supraventricular tachyarrhythmia in a hemodynamically stable patient, hypertension, and angina
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia, worsened cardiac output and marked constipation; blocks P-glycoprotein so digoxin levels rise toward toxicity

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade with intermediate potency — less vasodilation than the dihydropyridines but real nodal effects, with an IV onset around 3 minutes
drugs.indication: Rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, hypertension and angina when some nodal effect is wanted
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia and AV block; contraindicated with an IV beta blocker, in ventricular dysfunction, or with systolic pressure below 90 mmHg

drugs.name: Nifedipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine blockade of L-type channels in arteriolar smooth muscle only, with no effect on AV nodal conduction or the rate of channel recovery
drugs.indication: Hypertension and angina in extended-release form; also tocolysis for preterm labor at 24-34 weeks, limited to 48 hours
drugs.adverseEffects: Peripheral edema, headache and flushing; the immediate-release form causes reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated in unstable angina and STEMI

drugs.name: Amlodipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade with slow absorption and a 30-50 hour half-life, so plasma peaks and troughs are minimal
drugs.indication: First-line once-daily hypertension, where the flat concentration curve avoids the sympathetic reflex surges of short-acting agents
drugs.adverseEffects: Ankle edema — the most common side effect, caused by pre-capillary dilation with post-capillary reflex constriction, so diuretics do not help it

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.mechanism: Intravenous dihydropyridine producing arteriolar dilation with a rapid alpha-phase of about 3 minutes
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency, usually paired with labetalol or esmolol
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension with reflex tachycardia; the terminal half-life stretches to 14 hours after a long infusion

drugs.name: Clevidipine
drugs.mechanism: Ultra-short-acting intravenous dihydropyridine with a 1-minute half-life, allowing minute-to-minute titration
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency where tight, rapidly reversible control is needed; duration is only 5-15 minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Rebound hypertension on abrupt discontinuation; lipid emulsion vehicle

drugs.name: Nimodipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine with selectivity for cerebral arteries, available orally only with 13% bioavailability
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension; must never be given intravenously

drugs.name: Propranolol
drugs.mechanism: First-generation non-selective competitive antagonism of beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, with high lipid solubility and CNS penetration
drugs.indication: Angina, arrhythmia, hyperthyroid symptom control, and low-dose use an hour before performance anxiety
drugs.adverseEffects: Bronchospasm from beta-2 blockade in asthma or COPD, peripheral vascular insufficiency, fatigue, insomnia and nightmares

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.mechanism: Second-generation relatively beta-1 selective blockade, with selectivity that is dose-dependent and lost at higher doses
drugs.indication: One of only four beta blockers with proven mortality benefit in stable heart failure, plus post-MI and rate control
drugs.adverseEffects: Excessive bradycardia, delayed recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycemia with blunted warning symptoms, decreased insulin sensitivity

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.mechanism: Beta-1 selective blockade with a 9-minute half-life, given only as an intravenous infusion
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency and intraoperative tachycardia, where the drug must be able to disappear within minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension and bradycardia that resolve quickly on stopping the infusion

drugs.name: Carvedilol
drugs.mechanism: Third-generation non-selective beta blockade plus alpha-1 antagonism, calcium entry blockade and antioxidant activity
drugs.indication: HFrEF, where it is one of the four agents with proven mortality benefit; also hypertension
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension from the alpha-1 component, bradycardia, and bronchospasm from non-selective beta blockade

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.mechanism: Combined non-selective beta and alpha-1 blockade, available intravenously with a half-life around 5 hours
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency, and the recommended agent for hypertension in pregnancy
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, scalp tingling, bradycardia and bronchospasm

drugs.name: Nebivolol
drugs.mechanism: Third-generation beta-1 selective blockade that also stimulates nitric oxide production for vasodilation
drugs.indication: Hypertension and heart failure — one of the four beta blockers with proven mortality benefit
drugs.adverseEffects: Headache and fatigue; the vasodilating agents avoid the insulin-resistance penalty of the non-vasodilating ones

transporters.name: L-type Calcium Channel
transporters.location: Vascular smooth muscle, cardiac myocytes, and SA and AV nodal tissue
transporters.function: A slow, high-threshold channel that admits extracellular calcium and triggers calcium-induced calcium release; in smooth muscle the calcium-calmodulin complex activates MLCK, phosphorylating myosin light chains to produce contraction
transporters.regulation: Blockers bind the pore-forming alpha-1 subunit from the inner side of the membrane and prefer open and inactivated states, so the block deepens with stimulation frequency
transporters.inhibitor: Verapamil and diltiazem (heart and vessels), and the dihydropyridines (arteriolar smooth muscle)
